query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys that meet the minimum compositional requirements, superconductivity is primarily governed by the degree of lattice strain induced by atomic size mismatches. Moderate strain enhances electron–phonon coupling and increases the density of states at the Fermi level, thereby favoring superconducting pairing, whereas excessive strain leads to the nucleation of secondary precipitates that disrupt the superconducting state.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy with at least five elements (each ≥5 at.%) prepared using a powder metallurgy process that minimizes secondary phase formation.
generation.intervention: Systematically alter the alloy composition by substituting a small fraction of one element with another of a significantly different atomic radius to incrementally adjust the lattice strain.
generation.conditions: The alloy must remain in a disordered solid-solution state without significant phase separation (i.e. staying within processing conditions that avoid the precipitation observed at high additive contents such as high Al levels). Measurements of superconductivity should be conducted at temperatures low enough to resolve Tc changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The extent of lattice distortion, characterized by changes in lattice parameters and possible onset of secondary phase formation (as seen in the precipitation of intermetallic compounds in other HEAs), that mediates the electron–phonon coupling.
generation.mechanism: Increasing atomic size mismatch induces lattice strain that modifies the vibrational (phonon) spectrum. Up to a certain threshold, this enhanced strain strengthens electron–phonon interactions and the density of states at the Fermi level, favoring superconductivity. Beyond that threshold, the formation of secondary phases or precipitates (which act as scattering centers) can undermine superconductivity by breaking Cooper pairs.
generation.predicted_outcome: A systematic increase in lattice strain by controlled elemental substitution will initially lead to an increase in the superconducting critical temperature (Tc) relative to the baseline alloy. However, when the strain is too high and secondary phases begin to form, Tc will drop relative to the peak value observed.
generation.baseline: The original homogeneous, single‐phase HEA with moderate lattice strain that exhibits a certain critical temperature Tc.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold when the alloy remains in the solid solution state. If the atomic mismatch drives the system outside the single-phase regime (i.e. significant precipitation), the relationship will break down due to pair-breaking effects. The exact compositional window over which this applies remains to be determined.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative impact on Tc (an initial increase followed by a decrease) is expected, the precise magnitude of Tc shifts and the compositional thresholds for secondary precipitation are uncertain due to the complex interplay of disorder, electron scattering, and phase stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of HEA samples where a single element is gradually substituted by another with a larger atomic radius to induce incremental increases in lattice distortion. All samples should be processed under the same conditions (e.g., high-energy mechanical milling and sintering without high-pressure application) to ensure a similar baseline microstructure. Use X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to monitor phase purity and lattice constants, and measure the superconducting critical temperature (Tc) via low-temperature transport measurements.
measurements: XRD to quantify lattice parameter changes and identify any secondary phases
Electron microscopy (e.g., TEM/SEM) to assess microstructural homogeneity
Electrical resistivity or magnetic susceptibility measurements to determine Tc
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the systematic variation of lattice strain does not yield an initial correlation wherein moderate increases in strain lead to higher Tc (followed by a decrease in Tc upon secondary phase formation), then the hypothesis that lattice strain governs the superconducting behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Through the proposed methodology, involving high-energy mechanical milling combined with sintering without the application of pressure, it was possible to manufacture high entropy alloys of the CuCrFeNiTiAlx system. Here, the effect of Al on the microstructure, phase evolution, and chemical behavior of the resulting alloys was studied. The following are the main conclusions reached in this study: The powder metallurgy process was proven as an effective experimental route to retain the characteristic microstructure of high entropy alloys. Since milling induces a finer particle size and high lattice distortion, both conditions facilitate metal bonding in the solid state. Furthermore, sintering promotes metal diffusion and, consequently, their solubility and sample densification. Based on the XRD studies, as the Al concentration increases, high entropy alloys undergo a microstructural transformation, from a single FCC phase to a mixture of coexisting phases made of FCC and BCC phases, as well as the precipitation of different compounds such as FeNi, Al3Ni, CrNiFe, TiAl, and Ti3Al.
